info.description:
SaaS backend with Keycloak-issued JWT auth.
All protected endpoints require a Bearer token obtained from Keycloak.
info.title: Lightweight SaaS Backend API

get.description:
Returns a newest-first snapshot of the in-process audit
ring buffer. Process-local and volatile: events from other
replicas are not visible, and a restart drops the buffer.
The durable trail is the structured log stream.

parameters.description: max events to return (default: capacity; clamped to capacity)
parameters.name: limit

get.description:
Synthesizes an "invitations" view from Keycloak users whose
state implies an invitation: required actions pending, or
users carrying the `invited_by` user attribute (written by
POST /admin/users/invite when that lands in Stage B).

post.description:
Provisions a Keycloak user in invited-but-incomplete state,
assigns initial realm roles, and dispatches the action email
(VERIFY_EMAIL + UPDATE_PASSWORD). The new user is enabled but
cannot fully sign in until they complete both actions.
When the request body omits `invited_by`, the handler
defaults it to the authenticated admin's email (or sub).

400.description: invalid email, empty roles, past expires_at, etc.

404.description: one of the requested roles does not exist

409.description: a user with this email already exists

502.description: upstream identity provider unavailable (often: SMTP not configured)

delete.description:
Deletes the underlying Keycloak user. Guarded against
self-delete.

post.description:
Idempotent — re-dispatches the VERIFY_EMAIL + UPDATE_PASSWORD
action email. Returns the invitation as it stands now.

get.description:
Returns every realm role in the Keycloak realm. Client roles
are filtered out. Built-in roles (offline_access,
uma_authorization, default-roles-*) are flagged via the
`builtin` field so callers can disable destructive actions.

post.description:
Creates a new realm role in Keycloak. The service normalizes
the name (lowercase + trim) and rejects reserved names
(admin, user, offline_access, uma_authorization, default-roles-*).
Duplicates surface as 409.

400.description: invalid name (empty, too long, reserved, or bad characters)

delete.description:
Protected roles (admin, user, default-roles-*,
offline_access, uma_authorization) are rejected with 403.

patch.description:
Only the description field is mutable. Protected roles
(admin, user, default-roles-*, offline_access, uma_authorization)
are rejected with 403.

get.description:
Aggregates user-sessions across every enabled client in the
realm. A session that has touched multiple clients yields a
single entry whose `clients` map carries every client name.
One slow or failing client does not break the aggregation;
failures are silently skipped.
get.summary: List active sessions across the realm (admin)

get.description:
Returns a page of users from the Keycloak realm. Requires the
caller's token to carry the realm `admin` role. Pagination
is offset-based; `max` is clamped to [1, 100] server-side.

Returns a single user by Keycloak `sub` UUID. Requires the
caller's token to carry the realm `admin` role.

delete.description:
Guarded: refuses to delete your own account; refuses to
delete the last enabled admin.

patch.description:
Partial update — omitted fields are preserved. Guarded
against self-disable and last-admin removal. Returns the
updated user representation.

put.description:
Sets the user's Keycloak credential directly. When temporary=true
the user must change the password on next login.

post.description:
Queues UPDATE_PASSWORD as a required action and dispatches
the action email via Keycloak's execute-actions-email
endpoint. Requires realm SMTP to be configured (a 502
usually means it isn't).

Grants the named realm roles. Roles are resolved by name —
a missing role short-circuits with 404 before any
partial-assignment happens.
post.summary: Assign realm roles to a user (admin)

delete.description:
Guarded: refuses to remove your own admin role; refuses to
remove the last enabled admin.
delete.summary: Remove a realm role from a user (admin)

delete.description:
Logs the target user out of every client. Not blocked for
self-logout; an admin doing this to themselves invalidates
their current token too.
delete.summary: Revoke every session of a user (admin)

get.description: Equivalent to /health/live. Kept for existing deployments and monitors.

Returns 200 while the process is running. No auth, no dependency checks, no I/O.
A failure here means the process is wedged and should be restarted.

Returns 200 when this instance can serve traffic, 503 otherwise.
Checks only GLOBAL dependencies: the database, and whether a shutdown has begun.
A workspace whose Keycloak is down does NOT make the instance unready —
that request answers provider_unavailable and every other workspace keeps working.

Returns the local user record for the authenticated subject.
On first call for a new subject, JIT-creates the local row
from token claims (sub, email, preferred_username).

Advertises the scope vocabulary so a console does not hard-code
it and drift from the server. Adding a scope is a migration, so
this list changes rarely.

Mounted OUTSIDE the workspace path on purpose: the vocabulary is
a property of the installation, not of a workspace, and putting
it under `/projects/scopes` would also collide with the
`/projects/{project_id}` route in the router's tree.

**Operator only.**

Returns workspaces ordered by name, then id. By default only
active workspaces are returned — archived ones are operational
history rather than part of the working set. Requires the
caller's token to carry the realm `admin` role.

post.description:
Creates an active workspace. `slug` is optional: when omitted
it is derived from `name`. When supplied it is trimmed and
lowercased but never rewritten — an unusable slug is reported
rather than silently changed. Slugs are globally unique and are
never released, including by archiving.

get.description:
Returns one workspace by public id. Archived workspaces remain
individually readable. Accepts `ws_<uuid>`; a bare UUID is also
accepted as a development convenience.

patch.description:
Renames a workspace. `name` is the only mutable field: `slug`
is immutable, and `status` changes go through the archive
operation. Sending either is rejected rather than ignored, so a
client never believes a change took effect when it did not.
Archived workspaces cannot be modified.

post.description:
Moves a workspace to the archived state and stamps
`archived_at`. Idempotent: archiving an already-archived
workspace succeeds and returns it unchanged, so a retried
request is safe. Nothing is deleted, the slug is not released,
and there is no reactivation path.

get.description:
Returns the durable audit trail for this workspace, newest first.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `audit:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.

The trail records ATTEMPTS TO CHANGE STATE by an identified actor —
who did what, to which resource, whether it worked, and on which
request. It is not a request log: reads are absent, and so is
traffic that never got past authentication.

**Pagination is cursor-based.** Pass the `next_cursor` from the
previous page; its ABSENCE means there is no more history. Offset
pagination is not offered: this table only ever grows at the head,
so an offset shifts under a client between pages.

**This endpoint never returns secret material.** No password, no
credential secret or hash, no connection secret, no provider token,
and no request body — regardless of who is asking.

parameters.description: opaque cursor from the previous page
parameters.name: cursor

get.description:
Returns the workspace's connections ordered by name, then id.
Unlike the workspace listing, the default here is **all**
statuses: the operator workflow is draft → verify → activate →
the previous one retires, and hiding two thirds of that would
make the endpoint unusable. Client secrets are never returned.

post.description:
Creates a connection in **draft** state. The client secret is
sealed with AES-256-GCM before it reaches the database and is
never returned by any endpoint. A draft does nothing until it
has been verified and activated.

400.description: connection_name_required, connection_base_url_invalid, connection_realm_required, connection_client_id_required, connection_client_secret_required, connection_provider_unsupported, invalid_workspace_id, invalid_request

get.description: Returns one connection. The client secret is never included.

delete.description:
Permanently removes a **draft** or **retired** connection and
its sealed credential. An active connection cannot be deleted:
retire it first, so taking a workspace's provider out of
service is a visible, separate step.

patch.description:
Edits a **draft** connection's configuration. Changing
`base_url`, `realm`, `client_id` or `client_secret` resets the
verification — the stored verdict referred to coordinates that
no longer apply, and keeping it would let the connection be
activated on the strength of a probe against a different
provider. `status` and `provider` are rejected rather than
ignored: state changes go through activate and retire.

post.description:
Promotes a verified draft to **active** and retires the
workspace's previous active connection in the same transaction.
At most one connection per workspace is active, enforced by a
partial unique index rather than by application code.

Requires a verification that passed within the last hour.
Unlike archive, this is deliberately **not** idempotent: a
repeat call returns `connection_already_active`, because a
caller retrying may believe they are switching away from a
different connection.

409.description: connection_not_verified, connection_verification_expired, connection_already_active, connection_retired, workspace_archived, workspace_has_active_connection

post.description:
Moves a connection to **retired**, its terminal state. Works on
a draft or an active connection; retiring an active one leaves
the workspace with no active connection. There is no
reactivation path — create a new connection instead. Retiring an
already-retired connection is a conflict, not a no-op.

Probes the provider and records the verdict. The probe is
strictly read-only: it reaches the provider, confirms the realm
exists, authenticates the admin client, then reads the realm
settings and lists one user. It creates no test user and
modifies nothing.

The first three checks decide `health`. The two admin reads
decide `access_mode`: a service account that authenticates but
cannot read is `healthy` + `limited` — correctly configured and
under-privileged, which is a different fix from a wrong URL.

A successful verification authorizes activation for one hour.

200.description: the probe ran; check report.ok for the verdict

get.description:
Invitations are DERIVED from user state — Keycloak has no
invitation resource. A user with pending required actions or
invitation attributes appears here; once they complete those
actions they stop appearing, without anything being deleted.

`status` is computed: pending, accepted, expired or revoked.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `invitations:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.

post.description:
Provisions a user in invited-but-incomplete state, assigns the
requested realm roles, and dispatches Keycloak's action email.

REQUIRES SMTP configured on the workspace's realm. Without it
the email dispatch fails, and the half-provisioned user is
removed so the same address can be retried — you get an error,
not a silent half-invitation. Installations without SMTP should
use POST .../users instead, which sets a temporary password and
sends nothing.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `invitations:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
post.summary: Invite a user to a workspace's realm

502.description: provider_unavailable (includes SMTP not configured on the realm)

delete.description:
An invitation IS a user, so this deletes the user. Self-deletion
is refused; the last-admin guard does NOT apply here, because an
invited user cannot yet hold admin. To delete a user who has
accepted, use DELETE .../users/{user_id}, which is guarded.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `invitations:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.

parameters.description: the invited user's Keycloak sub UUID
parameters.name: invitation_id

post.description:
Only the still-pending actions are re-dispatched, so a user who
already verified their email is not asked to do it again.

An ACCEPTED invitation (nothing left to do) and a REVOKED one
(user disabled) both return `conflict` — the first has nothing
to resend, the second needs the user re-enabled first.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `invitations:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
post.summary: Re-send a workspace invitation's action email

parameters.description: the invited user's Keycloak sub UUID
parameters.name: invitation_id

502.description: provider_unavailable (includes SMTP not configured on the realm)

get.description:
Returns every project in the workspace, active and archived,
with a count of the credentials that can currently authenticate.
Archived projects are included because this listing backs a
management screen: hiding them would leave no way to confirm an
archive happened.

**Operator only.** No project credential can reach this route,
whatever scopes it holds.

post.description:
Creates an active project bound PERMANENTLY to this workspace.
The binding cannot be changed: it is the authorization boundary
every credential of this project is confined to. If another
workspace needs API access, create a project there.

Names are unique per workspace, compared case-insensitively.

**Operator only.**

get.description:
A project belonging to a different workspace reads as not found,
so an id cannot be used to confirm another workspace's contents.

**Operator only.**

patch.description:
Name is the only mutable field. `workspace_id` is declared in
the body solely so this endpoint can REFUSE it: moving a project
between workspaces would silently repoint every live credential
at a different realm, which is the one thing the authorization
model must never allow.

**Operator only.**

post.description:
Freezes the project. EVERY credential it holds stops
authenticating immediately — authentication reads the project's
status in the same lookup as the credential, so this is one
atomic kill switch rather than a loop over keys that could
half-finish.

Idempotent: archiving an already-archived project succeeds.

**Operator only.**

get.description:
Returns credential METADATA. The secret is never included, and
no endpoint can return it: only a SHA-256 digest is stored, so
the plaintext does not exist anywhere in this system after the
create call returned it.

Revoked credentials are included: the list is the trail an
operator reads when working out which key a deployment still
holds.

**Operator only.**

post.description:
Mints a machine credential and returns the secret **once**.
There is no endpoint that can show it again, and adding one
would be impossible without changing what is stored: only a
SHA-256 digest of the secret is persisted.

Scopes are explicit and non-empty. Nothing is granted by
default, and an empty list is rejected rather than treated as
"no permissions" — a credential that authenticates and can do
nothing is a configuration mistake worth reporting at creation.

A project may hold at most 10 active credentials. Rotation is
create-new, deploy, revoke-old.

**Operator only.**

Takes effect immediately: authentication reads the credential
row on every request and there is no cache to invalidate. A
request already in flight completes — it was authorized when it
started — but the next one fails.

Revoking an already-revoked credential is a conflict rather than
a silent success, so an operator learns that someone else got
there first.

**Operator only.**

get.description:
Returns the realm roles from the Keycloak realm that the
workspace's ACTIVE connection points at. Roles Keycloak manages
itself are returned with `builtin: true`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.

post.description:
Creates a realm role in the Keycloak realm that the workspace's
ACTIVE connection points at. The role appears in that realm and
in no other.

Names are trimmed and lowercased. Names the platform or Keycloak
manages (`admin`, `user`, `offline_access`, `uma_authorization`,
`default-roles-*`) are refused with `role_reserved`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
post.summary: Create a realm role in a workspace

get.description:
**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
get.summary: Get a realm role in a workspace

delete.description:
Protected roles return `role_reserved`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
delete.summary: Delete a realm role in a workspace

patch.description:
`description` is the only mutable field. Renaming is out of
scope: it would require rewriting every role-mapping that
references the old name. Protected roles return `role_reserved`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
patch.summary: Update a realm role's description in a workspace

get.description:
Pages through the full membership rather than returning
Keycloak's default first 100 — the last-admin guard depends on
seeing the complete set.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
get.summary: List the users carrying a realm role in a workspace

get.description:
Aggregates sessions client by client, so a realm with many
clients pays a per-client round trip. Realm-wide, not per-user —
for one user's sessions use the user-scoped route.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `sessions:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
get.summary: List active sessions across a workspace's realm

delete.description:
**Required scope (project credentials):** `sessions:revoke`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
delete.summary: Revoke a single session in a workspace

get.description:
Returns a page of users from the Keycloak realm that the
workspace's ACTIVE connection points at. The workspace id in the
path is the routing boundary: two workspaces connected to two
realms return two disjoint sets of users.

`first` and `max` in the response are the EFFECTIVE values —
what the server actually used after clamping `max` to [1, 100]
and `first` to >= 0. This differs from the legacy
`GET /admin/users`, which echoes the caller's raw input.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `users:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.

post.description:
Provisions a user directly with a temporary password they must
change on first login. This is the existing direct-provisioning
flow, not a new one — the alternative is an invitation, which
sends an email and therefore requires SMTP configured on the
realm.

If setting the password or assigning roles fails after the user
was created, the half-provisioned user is removed so the same
email can be retried.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `users:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
post.summary: Create a user in a workspace

get.description:
**Required scope (project credentials):** `users:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
get.summary: Get a user in a workspace

delete.description:
Guarded against self-deletion and against removing the realm's
last enabled admin; both return `caller_forbidden`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `users:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
delete.summary: Delete a user in a workspace

patch.description:
Partial update — omitted fields are preserved. Guarded against
self-disable and against disabling the realm's last enabled
admin; both return `caller_forbidden`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `users:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
patch.summary: Update a user in a workspace

put.description:
Sets the password without sending email. With
`temporary: true` Keycloak forces a change on next login.
Minimum 8 characters here; the realm's own password policy
applies on top and may reject more.

The password is never echoed, never logged, and never part of
the audit event this emits.
put.summary: Set a user's password directly in a workspace

post.description:
Dispatches Keycloak's UPDATE_PASSWORD action email. This is the
EMAIL flow, and it requires SMTP configured on the workspace's
realm — an unconfigured realm surfaces as `provider_unavailable`.
To set a password directly instead, use PUT .../password.

The two are exposed as separate routes on purpose: they have
different prerequisites and different outcomes, and hiding that
behind one endpoint with a flag would make failures unreadable.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `users:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
post.summary: Send a password-reset action email to a user in a workspace

get.description:
**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
get.summary: List a user's realm roles in a workspace

post.description:
Roles are resolved by name; a missing role short-circuits with
`role_not_found` before any partial assignment happens.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
post.summary: Grant realm roles to a user in a workspace

delete.description:
Guarded against removing your own `admin` role and against
removing it from the realm's last enabled admin; both return
`caller_forbidden`.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `roles:write`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
delete.summary: Revoke a realm role from a user in a workspace

get.description:
**Required scope (project credentials):** `sessions:read`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
get.summary: List one user's sessions in a workspace

delete.description:
Deliberately NOT guarded against self-logout: an admin logging
themselves out of other browsers is a valid recovery action, and
the worst case is they invalidate their own token too.

**Required scope (project credentials):** `sessions:revoke`.
Operators are authorized by the realm `admin` role instead.
delete.summary: Revoke all of a user's sessions in a workspace

project_id.description:
Project fields. ProjectID and CredentialID are the public `prj_` and
`key_` ids: the credential id is what an operator revokes, so an audit
line names the exact key to pull rather than the project that held it.

type.description:
Type is "operator" or "project". Empty only for an unattributed event
(no principal on the request), which is preserved as a visible gap
rather than defaulted to a plausible value.

metadata.description: Metadata is per-event detail, allowlisted per event type at write time.

reason_code.description:
ReasonCode is present only on a failure, and is drawn from the closed /v1
error vocabulary. It is never an upstream error message: the real cause
is in the log line for this request_id.

count.description:
Count is the number of items IN THIS PAGE, never a total. A total would
mean a second COUNT(*) over an append-heavy table on every request, to
answer a question no client here needs.

limit.description: Limit is the page size actually applied.

next_cursor.description:
NextCursor is absent on the last page.

Its ABSENCE is the end-of-history signal, not an empty page: a client
loops while this is present, so a correct client makes exactly as many
requests as there are pages.

detail.description:
Detail is a short human-readable explanation, safe to show an operator.
It never contains the client secret, the access token, or a provider
response body — a provider's error page can echo back anything.

name.description: Name is one of the Check* constants.

ok.description: OK is whether this specific probe passed.

access_mode.description:
AccessMode is what the service account was proven able to do.
`full` is claimed ONLY when write capability was positively proven —
see connection.AccessMode. A client may enable mutation controls on
`full` and must not on `read_only` or `limited`.

can_write.description:
CanWrite is AccessMode's write verdict, precomputed so a client does not
re-implement the rule (and get `unknown` wrong in either direction).
It is the field a UI should gate mutation controls on.

has_client_secret.description:
HasClientSecret reports that a credential is stored. It is always true
today because the column is NOT NULL; it exists as a field so that
clients render "secret configured" from the API rather than assuming,
and so the shape already fits if a secret-less auth method (mTLS,
private_key_jwt) is ever added.

verified.description:
Verified is IsVerified evaluated at response time: healthy AND the probe
is still inside its validity window. Computed rather than stored, because
it is a fact about now, not about the row — a client that stored it would
be wrong an hour later.

client_secret.description:
ClientSecret is write-only. It is sealed with AES-256-GCM before it
reaches the database and is never returned by any endpoint.

provider.description: Provider is optional while only one exists; omitted means keycloak.

message.example: Connection must pass verification before it can be activated

access_mode.description: AccessMode is what the admin client turned out to be allowed to do.

checked_at.description: CheckedAt is when the run completed.

checks.description:
Checks are in execution order, and stop at the first failure that makes
later ones meaningless (no point listing users if the token failed).

ok.description: OK is the verdict that drives Health. See Verifier for what it requires.

summary.description:
Summary is a one-line verdict for logs and for the connection's
health_message.
summary.example: provider reachable, realm found, client authenticated, full admin access

count.description: length of users array, NOT total

expires_at.description: ExpiresAt is optional, RFC 3339, and must be in the future.

invited_by.description: InvitedBy defaults to the authenticated caller when omitted.

roles.description:
Roles is REQUIRED and must contain at least one existing realm role name.
Unlike CreateUserRequest, where roles can be granted afterwards, an
invitation with no roles would invite someone to an account that can do
nothing.
Roles is optional: realm role names to grant at creation.

temporary_password.description:
TemporaryPassword is REQUIRED and must be at least 8 characters. There is
no way to create a user without choosing a credential for them; the
alternative is an invitation, which needs working SMTP on the realm.

It is never echoed back, never logged, and never part of an audit event.

field.description:
Field names the request field a validation failure is about.

`omitempty`, and that is the compatibility contract: an error that is not
about a field carries no key at all, so a client written before this
existed decodes every response exactly as it did. Adding a key is safe;
adding one that is sometimes an empty string is not, because it invites
`if err.Field == ""` to be read as "no field" in one place and "field is
blank" in another.

Set only for `invalid_request`. Never derived from client input.

temporary.description:
Temporary forces a change on next login. Defaults to false, so an
omitted field sets a permanent password — the caller must opt in to
the friction rather than out of it.

expires_at.description: ExpiresAt is optional. When set it must be in the future.

label.description: Label is required. An unlabelled key is one nobody dares revoke.

scopes.description:
Scopes must be non-empty and drawn from the supported vocabulary. There
is no default and nothing is implied: a credential's power is always an
explicit choice.

secret.description: Secret is the full token, e.g. lw_sk_<lookup>_<secret>. Shown once.

key_prefix.description:
KeyPrefix is the lookup segment of the token, e.g. "k3mzr7q2xwab5f9d".
Shown so an operator can match a key in a log line to a row here.

status.description:
Status is the credential's effective state, computed at response time:
active, expired or revoked. Computed rather than stored because expiry is
a fact about now, not about the row.

active_credentials.description:
ActiveCredentials is how many credentials can currently authenticate.
Included in the listing so an operator can see at a glance which projects
hold live keys without opening each one.

name.description: Name is required and must be non-blank after trimming.

slug.description:
Slug is optional. When omitted it is derived from Name; when present it
is only trimmed and lowercased, never slugified — an unusable slug is
reported rather than silently rewritten.

archived_at.description:
ArchivedAt is null for active workspaces and set for archived ones. The
database enforces that this and Status can never disagree.

id.description:
ID is always the prefixed form, `ws_<uuid>`. The bare UUID is never
exposed.

BearerAuth.description: OPERATOR authentication. Type "Bearer" followed by a Keycloak-issued access token. The token must carry the realm `admin` role, which is re-checked against the provider on every request.
BearerAuth.name: Authorization

ProjectKeyAuth.description: PROJECT authentication (machine-to-machine). Type "Bearer" followed by a project credential, e.g. `Bearer lw_sk_<lookup>_<secret>`. The credential is bound to exactly one workspace and carries an explicit scope set; the scope each operation requires is stated in its description. Control-plane operations (workspaces, connections, projects) are operator-only and answer `operator_only` to any credential. Swagger 2.0 cannot express per-operation scopes for an apiKey scheme, so they are documented in prose rather than declared — see docs/PROJECTS.md.
ProjectKeyAuth.name: Authorization
